paper_metadata.title: Algorithm for pricing Asian-style FX options on a gate-based quantum computer

summary: The paper implements a gate‑based quantum Monte Carlo algorithm for pricing an Asian EUR/PLN option using distribution loading, QFT‑based averaging, payoff encoding, and amplitude estimation. Experiments on a Qiskit statevector simulator with M=4 time points and N=3 discretization qubits produced prices close to classical Monte Carlo for most strikes (e.g., 140,896.63 classical vs 141,219.63 quantum for strike 4.6265), but QAE results were unstable and deviated significantly for deep out‑of‑the‑money options (e.g., 3,579.75 classical vs 27,998.4 QAE at strike 5.0892).

experiments.description: Gate-based quantum Monte Carlo / amplitude-estimation pricing of an Asian FX call option on EUR/PLN using distribution loading, QFT-based mean calculation, comparator, payoff encoding, and iterative amplitude estimation; evaluated against classical Monte Carlo for multiple strikes and parameter settings.

algorithm.variant: Quantum Monte Carlo for Asian FX option pricing with QFT-based adder and Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE)
algorithm.convergence_criteria: IAE configured with target accuracy epsilon=0.001 and confidence alpha=0.05
algorithm.parameter_initialization: Not reported; distribution and pricing parameters are fixed from market data and chosen strike scenarios

problem_formulation.encoding_details: Each EUR/PLN price at each time point is discretized into 2^N intervals using N=3 qubits per time point; the arithmetic mean is computed in a larger register of size N+log2(M); comparator flags whether the averaged price exceeds the strike; payoff is encoded into ancilla amplitude; IAE estimates the payoff probability.
problem_formulation.objective_function: Price of an arithmetic-average Asian call option: payoff max(A_T - K, 0), with A_T = (1/M) sum_{i=1}^M S_{t_i}; final option value obtained from discounted expected payoff.
problem_formulation.constraints_handling: Comparator circuit and controlled rotations implement the strike threshold and payoff truncation; no explicit penalty formulation.

problem_instance.description: EUR/PLN Asian currency option pricing under Black-Scholes-Merton dynamics with time-dependent domestic/foreign rates and volatility; four observation dates over one year.

dataset_specification.preprocessing: Model parameters set as rd=[2.79%, 3.383%, 3.596%, 3.661%], rf=[-0.61%, -0.551%, -0.491%, -0.430%], sigma=[6.036%, 6.275%, 6.146%, 6.607%], S0=4.6265; low/high chosen as mu±3sigma at maturity; discretization into 2^N bins.

problem_instance.data_preprocessing_details: Lognormal path probabilities generated from the BSM model; discretization of exchange rates into intervals; mapping to qubit indices; local volatility extension discussed.
problem_instance.evaluation_methodology: Compared classical Monte Carlo, discretization-only, statevector-based quantum evaluation, and QAE-based evaluation across five strikes; additional sensitivity study for strike 5.0892 with c in {0.05,0.01} and N in {3,4}.

implementation_details.classical_solver: Classical Monte Carlo (Euler–Maruyama path simulation) used as the primary baseline; Qiskit statevector simulator used to compute exact amplitudes before applying QAE; QAE variants tested include Iterative Amplitude Estimation (IAE), Maximum Likelihood Amplitude Estimation (MLAE), and Faster Amplitude Estimation (FAE), with IAE used for reported experiments.
implementation_details.classical_preprocessing: Generate BSM path probabilities; discretize exchange-rate distribution; compute classical Monte Carlo benchmark and discretization-only benchmark.
implementation_details.classical_postprocessing: Convert estimated ancilla |1> probability to option price using price = fmax*(p^{-1/2}/c + 1/2) as reported; compare against classical Monte Carlo.

speedup_claims.conditions: amplitude estimation / quantum Monte Carlo pricing of derivatives
speedup_claims.caveats: Claimed in the literature and discussed in the paper; not directly benchmarked as a runtime speedup in this experiment.

complexity_analysis.quantum_complexity: Quadratic speed-up over classical Monte Carlo is claimed for amplitude estimation; no explicit asymptotic formula beyond that.
complexity_analysis.classical_complexity: Monte Carlo error scales as O(1/sqrt(M)) in number of samples.

advantage_assessment.crossover_size: Not reported; algorithm evaluated only for a toy instance with M=4 time steps and N=3 discretization qubits.
advantage_assessment.resources_for_advantage: Would require large-scale fault‑tolerant quantum computers capable of implementing deep circuits for distribution loading, arithmetic (QFT-based addition across hundreds of time steps in practical Asian options), and amplitude estimation with many Grover iterations.
limiting_factors: Experiments performed only on simulators with extremely small discretization (N=3 qubits per time step).
Amplitude estimation circuits require deep Grover iterations not feasible on NISQ hardware.
Probability distribution loading for stochastic paths scales poorly with number of time steps.
QAE results reported in Table 3 are unstable and often far from classical Monte Carlo estimates.

notes: hardware.type inferred as simulator_other because the paper reports Qiskit statevector simulator usage and does not name a real QPU; the experiments are presented as simulator-based evaluations.

num_qubits not explicitly summarized as a single total in the paper; inferred from the described registers (distribution loading with N=3 qubits for each of M=4 time points, mean register of N+log2(M)=5 qubits, comparator ancilla register, payoff qubit, and QAE ancillas), but exact total circuit qubit count is not stated in one place.

The paper explicitly states the use of IAE, MLAE, and FAE, but the main experimental focus and reported results are for IAE/statevector/QAE evaluation; no hardware execution on a physical device is described.
The authors claim a theoretical quadratic speed‑up from quantum amplitude estimation over classical Monte Carlo but explicitly evaluate only on simulators.
No hardware experiment or runtime comparison demonstrating practical speedup is provided.
